title: Evaluating AI Agent Skill Performance with NVIDIA SkillEvaluator | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA's open-source SkillEvaluator benchmarked over 300 verified 'agent skills' across 30+ NVIDIA products on Codex and Claude Code, finding an average Skill Lift of +31 points overall (+39 excluding Security), with Correctness rising from 46 to 87 and Effectiveness from 39 to 78 -- and finding that which product/domain a skill covers matters more to performance gains than which agent harness runs it.

insights.claim: NVIDIA verified Skills are packaged, signed capability descriptors that tell an AI agent what an NVIDIA product does, when to invoke it, and how to call it; SkillEvaluator measures their impact via a three-tier process: Tier 1 static safety/structure checks (schema, security scanning for prompt injection/data exfiltration, secret/PII detection, license, linting), Tier 2 embedding-similarity distinctiveness analysis to catch duplicated or overlapping guidance, and Tier 3 live agent task runs in isolated sandboxes with and without the skill installed.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: Establishes a formal, reusable evaluation methodology for the emerging 'agent skills' category -- relevant to any company building or curating a skills marketplace/catalog, as NVIDIA is effectively defining a quality bar (three-tier safety + performance evaluation) that competitors and skill marketplaces may need to match.

insights.claim: Tier 3 live evaluations use Harbor, an open-source framework for repeatable isolated-sandbox agent evaluations; for each case, an agent harness runs twice (once with the skill installed, once without) with identical prompt, model, task inputs, and grading criteria, and the score difference is reported as Skill Lift in points across two independent harnesses.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: A controlled A/B methodology (single variable: skill installed or not) gives the Skill Lift numbers causal credibility rather than being correlational marketing claims.

insights.claim: NVIDIA distributes its verified skills through multiple channels: its own plugins for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, as well as third-party marketplaces Skills.sh, ClawHub, and Hermes Hub.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: Shows NVIDIA is distributing developer-facing agent skills broadly across the major coding-agent ecosystems rather than favoring one, positioning NVIDIA as an infrastructure/content layer across competing agent platforms.
insights.locator: NVIDIA publishes plugins for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor

themes.theme: Benchmark results: Skill Lift across 300+ skills

insights.claim: Without any skill installed, agents across the NVIDIA/skills catalog (evaluated on Codex and Claude Code) scored between 39 and 46 out of 100 on Correctness, Discoverability, Effectiveness, and Efficiency, but 97 on Security -- indicating agents already avoid unsafe actions by default but struggle to complete specialized NVIDIA-product tasks correctly or efficiently without guidance.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: Quantifies the baseline capability gap general-purpose coding agents have on specialized NVIDIA-product tasks, framing the addressable value that a skills catalog is meant to close.

insights.claim: With verified skills installed, average scores rose from 46 to 87 on Correctness (+41 points), 42 to 82 on Discoverability (+40), 39 to 78 on Effectiveness (+39), 43 to 78 on Efficiency (+35), and 97 to 98 on Security (+1), yielding an overall average Skill Lift of +31 points across all dimensions and +39 points excluding Security.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: A headline, benchmarked quantification (+31 to +39 points on a 100-point scale) of the value NVIDIA's verified-skills program adds to agent task performance -- a concrete metric for evaluating whether 'agent skills' as a category deliver measurable ROI versus being a marketing layer.
insights.locator: Table 2. Average Skill Lift from verified skills

insights.claim: Skill Lift varies more by agent harness than the raw scores might suggest but the effect is modest: Claude Code shows +34 points average Skill Lift across all dimensions (+42 excluding Security) versus OpenAI Codex's +29 (+36 excluding Security) -- a roughly 5-point harness gap the authors attribute to differing default system prompts, context handling, and tool-calling implementations.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: Suggests verified skills provide somewhat larger performance uplift on Claude Code than on Codex, a data point relevant to comparing agent-harness quality/ecosystem maturity, though the authors emphasize the harness gap is secondary to product/domain effects.

insights.claim: Per-product Skill Lift ranges far more widely (roughly +2 to +46 points) than the harness-level difference (~5 points between Claude Code and Codex), leading NVIDIA to conclude that the product domain, task, and evaluation design matter more to Skill Lift than which agent harness runs the skill.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: A contrarian-to-the-hype finding: agent-harness choice (which coding-agent vendor you use) matters less to skill effectiveness than how well the skill itself is engineered for its specific domain -- implying investment should flow toward skill-authoring quality/evaluation datasets rather than harness selection.
insights.locator: The product matters more than the agent

insights.claim: Token and execution-time savings from skills are not automatic and vary by skill: the jetson-optimize-memory skill reduced tokens from 617,306 to 142,540 (-76.9%) and execution time from 474.9 to 220.0 seconds (-53.7%), while the cuopt-install skill instead increased tokens from 25,227 to 55,582 (+120.3%) and execution time from 34.0 to 41.1 seconds (+20.8%), in each case based on a single-attempt example.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts an assumption that skills always reduce token/compute cost -- some skills increase agent token spend even while improving correctness, meaning skill ROI must be evaluated per-skill on cost as well as quality; a caution for anyone assuming agent skills are a pure cost-reduction lever.

insights.claim: Better evaluation datasets produce better skills: teams that clearly define important tasks, expected outputs, and out-of-scope requests before running any agent produce sharper evaluation signals, since a skill's measured quality is bounded by how precisely its evaluation set describes the job.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: A practical guidance point for organizations building their own skill/tool libraries for AI agents: invest in eval-dataset design upfront rather than treating it as an afterthought.
insights.locator: Better evaluation datasets produce better skills

insights.claim: Third-party platforms are piloting SkillEvaluator: OpenClaw runs Tier 3 evaluations and displays with/without-skill results in an Evals tab on ClawHub, and Nous Research tested SkillEvaluator in Hermes Agent with an optional advisory scan by SkillSpector (checking PII, Unicode smuggling, script linting, license, and security issues) covered by 29 passing tests, with each skill scan taking approximately 1.4-1.5 seconds.
insights.speaker: Moshe Abramovitch
insights.so_what: Shows early third-party ecosystem adoption of NVIDIA's evaluation methodology beyond NVIDIA's own skills catalog, suggesting SkillEvaluator could become a de facto standard/interoperability layer for the broader agent-skills marketplace ecosystem.
